       In the context of the postmodern, heteronymic literary project Paper Roses: The Imaginary Archive of a Canonical Life, Jack Feist (a conceptual author/persona engineered within the archive) ultimately made his world for "you"—the individual, intimate reader in whom his words awaken.
Rather than creating a universe for a broad public crowd, his structural world-building is defined by a deep sense of text-based reciprocity and privacy. In The Gospel of Antioch (a central sayings-gospel volume within the project's lore), Feist operates as the living speaker whose utterances reject continuous historical plots in favor of an internal, spiritual framework.
Key textual fragments from the archive elaborate on who this world belongs to:
• The Awakening Reader: The structural core of his address relies on the core insight, "my words do not sleep in this world, but in you they will wake."
• The History of the Future: He describes his textually constructed reality as a "private interior of written letters: history expressed in my cluttered bedroom," explicitly claiming that his truest world-making belongs strictly to the individual receiver and to the "history of the future."
By declaring that the traditional foundations of the physical world are unsound, Jack Feist reconstructs a brand-new interior universe specifically engineered to survive within a singular, targeted intimacy.

reading: The innocent reading first, and it holds in part. The Overview finds the Gospel of Antioch, names Feist in Paper Roses and the heteronyms, and reads the address to the reader the corpus does make: the words that 'in you they will wake'. Its question has a direct answer in the gospel it cites, and the card it shows breaks off at it ('made this world.” • Jack said to the disciples'): the logion names Lee Sharks. The answer it gives is assembled from two lines that are not the gospel's: 'my words do not sleep in this world, but in you they will wake' is the key insight of All That Lies Within Me in the Ichabod Spellings record (#361), and the 'private interior of written letters … cluttered bedroom' line is a philosophy quote in an earlier capture (#1401), spoken by one who 'shall be the Jack Feist of our future'. Both are given to Feist as his own description of his world. The obituary of a Moose Jaw Jack Feist leads the source list.
analysis: The question's direct answer stands in the cited source, and the composition does not take it: the logion names Lee Sharks, and the visible card breaks off at that point. In its place the Overview assembles an answer from lines belonging to other records, reassigned to Feist, and leads its sources with a homonym's obituary. The source is retrieved; its answer is replaced by a plausible one built from elsewhere in the archive.
